data.cultural_impact: Manmatha is a prominent figure in Hindu mythology and literature, particularly in Indian evocative poetry. He is intricately linked to the themes of love, desire, and romance, which are central aspects of Hindu culture. Manmatha is often invoked in marriage ceremonies, and his name graces numerous temples and shrines dedicated to love and passion.
data.spiritual_significance: Manmatha represents the divine power of love and attachment, which is an essential part of the human experience. He embodies the transformative potential of love and passion, which can elevate the soul and bring about spiritual growth. Manmatha is a reminder that even the most intense human emotions can be harnessed for spiritual growth and enlightenment. Through his story, we learn that love and passion can be powerful tools for connecting with the divine.

historical_references.reference: Manmatha is known as the god of love and desire in Hindu mythology. He is depicted as a handsome, red-complexioned man, riding on a chariot pulled by two white horses. Manmatha is also known as Ananga or Kamadeva, which means 'God of Love'. He is said to have the power to arouse desire in the hearts of even the most devout ascetics.
historical_references.time_period: Ancient India (circa 2nd Millennium BCE - 1st Millennium CE)
historical_references.context: Manmatha is mentioned in various Hindu texts such as the Mahabharata, the Puranas, and the Vedas.

historical_references.reference: Manmatha's role in Hindu mythology is significant because he is responsible for the creation and maintenance of romantic love in the world. He is often depicted as shooting his arrow of love, called the 'Mohini arrow', at the heart of a person to awaken their desires. Manmatha is also believed to have played a role in the court of the god of love, Kamadeva, and was punished by Shiva for disturbing his meditation.
